short: A junior heraldic officer.
note: An officer of arms below the rank of herald, performing similar ceremonial and heraldic duties. The word also means a follower or attendant.

short: A pilgrim to the Holy Land.
note: A pilgrim who has visited the Holy Land, traditionally wearing crossed palm leaves as a sign of the journey.

short: Of Paphos; an old term for a sex worker.
note: Belonging to Paphos in Cyprus. In older English, a paphian can mean a female sex worker, and the adjective can describe illicit love.

short: A mountain nymph.
note: A nymph of hills or mountains in Greek mythology; the name comes from Greek oros, mountain.

short: Church property supporting a religious household.
note: Relating to a table; historically also applied to a church or property whose revenues maintained a bishop’s table or household. From Latin mensa, table.

short: A Parisian seamstress or shopgirl.
note: A traditional French name for a young Parisian seamstress or shop assistant.

short: An azure-blue phosphate mineral.
note: A blue mineral containing aluminum, magnesium, iron, and phosphate. Its name recalls the color of lapis lazuli.

short: Fine, downy body hair.
note: A soft, downy covering of hair, especially the hair of a mammalian fetus. Latin lanugo means down and is related to lana, wool.

short: A helmet scarf or decorative valance.
note: A cloth draped over a helmet; also a short decorative hanging along the top of a window or the edge of a shelf.

short: A glasslike form of opal.
note: A usually colorless variety of opal with a glasslike appearance, sometimes cloudy or whitish.

short: Irregular or unconventional.
note: Departing from customary forms or rules. In grammar, a heteroclite is a word with irregular inflection.

short: The six days of Creation.
note: The six days of Creation in Genesis; from Greek words meaning six and day.

short: A yellow pigment from tree resin.
note: A resin obtained from Garcinia trees of Southeast Asia and used as a yellow pigment; also the strong yellow color itself.

short: A great magician.
note: An eminent magician or enchanter; from Greek elements meaning chief and magus.

short: A dawn song or poem.
note: A poem or musical piece associated with daybreak, particularly a song of lovers separating at dawn.

short: An ominous spectral dog or goblin.
note: A ghost or goblin in English folklore, often appearing as a large dog and regarded as an omen of misfortune.

short: The mineral of emerald and aquamarine.
note: A hard mineral composed of beryllium aluminum silicate. Its colored varieties include emerald, aquamarine, heliodor, and morganite.

short: Shimmering like a cat’s eye.
note: Showing a shifting, luminous band as the surface turns, especially in a gemstone; from French chatoyer, to shine like a cat’s eyes.

short: Cordovan leather.
note: An old English name for cordovan leather, with a word history running through French to Spanish cordobán.

short: Latin: a leader or commander.
note: Latin dux means leader. In the later Roman Empire it became a title for a provincial military commander.

short: A thick, shaggy woolen cloth.
note: A heavy woolen fabric with a rough surface, used for protective outer clothing; also a garment made from it.

short: A German mercenary foot soldier.
note: A German infantry mercenary of the fifteenth to seventeenth centuries; from German Landsknecht. The word also names an old card game.

short: A vessel displaying the Eucharist.
note: A vessel designed to display the consecrated Eucharistic host for veneration. The name is related to Latin monstrare, to show.

short: Glowing or visible at night.
note: Shining or becoming visible at night; also used for organisms that produce light.

short: People whose shadows turn all around them.
note: An old geographical term, also spelled periscii, for people within a polar circle whose shadows sweep around them during the continuous daylight of summer.

short: Mandrake, a plant of magical folklore.
note: Mandrake: a Mediterranean plant of the nightshade family whose forked root can resemble a human figure and was traditionally credited with magical powers.

short: Open to the sky.
note: Hypaethral: having a central space open to the sky, especially a temple with an uncovered interior.

short: Possibly burgonet, a Renaissance helmet.
note: Possibly burgonet, a close-fitting helmet with cheek guards used in the sixteenth century.

short: A short medieval coat of mail.
note: A coat of mail generally shorter than a hauberk; also spelled habergeon.

short: Possibly Greek chrysos: gold.
note: Possibly Greek chrysos (χρυσός), gold, also used collectively for objects made from gold.

short: Latin: copper, bronze, or money.
note: Latin aes means copper or bronze and, by extension, objects made from those metals, including money.

sources.label: Lewis and Short Latin dictionary · Perseus

short: Possibly dimachae: cavalry fighting on foot.
note: Possibly dimachae, Macedonian troops trained to fight both on horseback and as infantry.

sources.label: Anthony Rich · Dictionary of Greek and Roman Antiquities

short: Possibly vintenar: leader of twenty soldiers.
note: Possibly vintenar, a medieval English officer commanding a vintaine, a unit nominally of twenty soldiers whose actual strength varied.

sources.label: University of Liverpool · study of medieval military levies

short: A religious company in ancient Greece.
note: A company or association gathered for religious celebration in ancient Greece, particularly the singing and dancing associated with Dionysus.

short: An old French battle trumpet.
note: An Old French and Anglo-Norman word for a horn or trumpet used to give signals in battle.

short: An extinct giant soaring bird.
note: Teratornis is a genus of large extinct birds. Teratornis merriami, found at La Brea, resembled a condor and exceeded the California condor in size.

sources.label: Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County · La Brea Tar Pits

short: A North African hooded robe.
note: An older form of djellaba, a loose outer robe with a hood, associated especially with North Africa.

short: Adriatic Slavs; Venetian mercenary troops.
note: An old Italian name for the Slavic peoples of the eastern Adriatic, also used for Slav soldiers serving the Republic of Venice.

short: A small auxiliary knife.
note: French bâtardeau: a small knife or dagger carried in the sheath of a larger dagger or sword.

short: Possibly Panthera atrox, the American lion.
note: Possibly Panthera atrox, the extinct American lion, a large Ice Age cat. Latin atrox means fierce or frightful.

sources.label: Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County · La Brea Tar Pits

short: An Egyptian term for the shadow.
note: An older Egyptological transcription for a person’s shadow, treated as a constituent of the person in ancient Egyptian religious accounts.

sources.label: E. A. Wallis Budge · introduction to the Book of the Dead

short: Possibly phrontisterion: a place for thought.
note: Possibly Greek phrontisterion, a place for thinking or study; Aristophanes uses the name for Socrates’ school in The Clouds.

short: Possibly the noctule bat; also French for a brief note.
note: Possibly noctule, the common name of Nyctalus noctula, a large bat with long, narrow wings. French notule also means a short note or annotation, from Latin notula, little mark.

short: Darkening or tending toward black.
note: Becoming black, blackish, or approaching black in color; from Latin nigrescere, to grow black.

sources.label: Noah Webster · American Dictionary of the English Language (1828)

short: Latin: a seer, prophet, or poet.
note: Latin vates means a prophet or seer; it also denotes a poet, linking poetry with inspired utterance.

short: Latin: sand or an arena.
note: Latin harena means sand, and also the sand-covered place of combat in an amphitheater, the source of English arena.

short: Latin: a eunuch.
note: A Latin word for a eunuch or, more broadly, someone regarded as incapable of procreation. It also described unfruitful plants.

short: An interpreter of lightning omens.
note: A priest who interpreted omens from lightning in ancient Rome; Latin fulgurator can also mean one who hurls lightning.

short: Latin: a trident.
note: A three-pronged spear or trident, associated with Neptune and used by the net-fighting gladiators called retiarii.

short: Possibly Latin hasta: spear or lance.
note: Possibly Latin hasta, a spear or lance. The word also served as a symbol of military and magisterial authority.

short: A many-headed sea monster of Greek myth.
note: A monster inhabiting the rocks opposite Charybdis. In Homer’s Odyssey she has six heads on long necks and snatches sailors from vessels passing her cave.

short: A visible appearance of a deity.
note: A manifestation in which a god becomes visible. The word comes through Greek theophaneia, combining the divine with the idea of appearing.

short: Possibly Aemilian, a name borne by several saints.
note: Possibly Aemilian, also spelled Emilian, a name borne by several Christian saints. They include a Spanish hermit remembered as San Millán and a bishop of Cyzicus who opposed iconoclasm.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Saint Trason, a Roman martyr.
note: Possibly Saint Trason, a Roman Christian remembered for helping imprisoned believers during Diocletian’s persecution. He was subsequently executed with his companions.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Saint Kyrin, also called Boniface.
note: Possibly Saint Kyrin, also called Kyrstin or Boniface, an early medieval bishop associated with Ross in Scotland.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Timon, one of the seven chosen in Acts.
note: Possibly Timon, named in Acts 6:5 among the seven men chosen to oversee the community’s charitable distribution. Christian tradition counts them as the first deacons.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Saint Cynog, son of Brychan of Brycheiniog.
note: Possibly Saint Cynog, or Canog, a Welsh saint traditionally regarded as a son of Brychan of Brycheiniog. His name is preserved in the place-name Merthyr Cynog.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Saint Caesidius, a martyr near Lake Fucino.
note: Possibly Saint Caesidius, a priest traditionally commemorated among Christians killed near Lake Fucino in central Italy during the Roman persecutions.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Sulpicius, the name of saints of Bourges.
note: Possibly Sulpicius, a name borne by several Christian saints, including two early bishops of Bourges. The later bishop, Sulpicius the Pious, is the namesake of Saint-Sulpice in Paris.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Saint Pelagia, a martyr of Antioch.
note: Possibly Saint Pelagia of Antioch, a young Christian martyr praised by Ambrose and John Chrysostom. She is distinct from the penitent of the same name also associated with Antioch.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Saint Olegarius, bishop of Barcelona and Tarragona.
note: Possibly Saint Olegarius, also called Ollegarius or Olaguer, an Augustinian canon who became bishop of Barcelona and archbishop of Tarragona in the twelfth century.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Saint Nympha, remembered with Tryphon and Respicius.
note: Possibly Saint Nympha, an early Christian saint whose relics were venerated in Rome. Her commemoration became associated with those of Tryphon and Respicius; little reliable biography survives.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Saint Minias, the martyr honored at San Miniato.
note: Possibly Saint Minias, or Miniato, a Christian martyr honored at Florence. His traditional life places his death in the persecution under Decius in the third century.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Saint Nidan, an early Welsh saint.
note: Possibly Saint Nidan, also called Midan, an early saint associated with Anglesey in Wales. Reliable details of his life are scarce.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Saint Memorius, a deacon of Troyes.
note: Possibly Saint Memorius, also called Mesmin or Nemorius, a deacon of Troyes. Tradition says he and his companions were killed during Attila’s invasion of Gaul.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Saint Menas, the Egyptian soldier-martyr.
note: Possibly Saint Menas, also spelled Mennas, an Egyptian soldier commemorated as a martyr under Diocletian.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Saint Lelia, an Irish saint of Munster.
note: Possibly Saint Lelia, an early Irish saint associated with the regions of Limerick and Kerry. Her memory survives in local dedications, although her biography is largely lost.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Saint Cyneburh, a Mercian princess and abbess.
note: Possibly Saint Cyneburh, also called Kyneburga, a daughter of King Penda of Mercia. She is traditionally associated with a religious community at Castor near Peterborough.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Saint Ivo, namesake of St Ives in Cambridgeshire.
note: Possibly Saint Ivo, a saint traditionally described as a Persian bishop who settled in England. His relics were enshrined at Ramsey Abbey, and St Ives in Cambridgeshire bears his name.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Saint Gwinoc, a Welsh monk associated with poetry.
note: Possibly Saint Gwinoc, a Welsh monastic saint traditionally associated with early Welsh poetry.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Saint Blathmac, an abbot killed at Iona.
note: Possibly Saint Blathmac, also called Blaithmaic, an Irish abbot killed by Viking raiders at Iona in the ninth century. Walahfrid Strabo commemorated him in a Latin poem.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Saint Bega, namesake of St Bees.
note: Possibly Saint Bega, also called Bee, an early saint traditionally said to have come from Ireland to Cumberland. St Bees and St Bees Head preserve her name.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Saint Aphrodisius, a martyr of North Africa.
note: Possibly Saint Aphrodisius, commemorated with Peter among the Christians persecuted by the Arian Vandals in North Africa. The surviving records leave his dates and identity uncertain.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Saint Zambdas, an early bishop of Jerusalem.
note: Possibly Saint Zambdas, a bishop of Jerusalem around the beginning of the fourth century.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Saint Irais, an Egyptian martyr.
note: Possibly Saint Irais, also called Herais or Rhais, an Egyptian Christian martyr. Her traditional life describes her voluntarily joining prisoners being taken by boat to execution.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Saint Vodalus, an early medieval hermit.
note: Possibly Saint Vodalus, also called Vodoaldus or Voel, an Irish or Scottish monk remembered as a missionary in Gaul and a hermit near Soissons.

sources.label: Catholic Church in Norway · Saint Vodalus

short: Possibly Blessed Sancha, a Portuguese princess and nun.
note: Possibly Blessed Sancha, a daughter of King Sancho I of Portugal who adopted a monastic life at Alenquer and later retired to the monastery of Celas near Coimbra.

short: Possibly Blessed Mafalda, a Portuguese princess and Cistercian.
note: Possibly Blessed Mafalda, a daughter of King Sancho I of Portugal. After an annulled marriage to the king of Castile, she became a Cistercian at Arouca.

short: Possibly Saint Gerbold, bishop of Bayeux.
note: Possibly Saint Gerbold, also called Gerbaud, a bishop of Bayeux in the late seventh century. Tradition connects him with the foundation of Livry Abbey in Normandy.

short: Possibly Quartillosa, a Christian martyr of Carthage.
note: Possibly Quartillosa, a Christian woman commemorated among the third-century martyrs of Carthage, together with her husband and son.

sources.label: French Bishops’ Conference · Martyrs of Carthage

short: Possibly Blessed Josepha Maria of Benigànim.
note: Possibly Blessed Josepha Maria of Benigànim, born Inés Albiñana, a seventeenth-century Discalced Augustinian nun in eastern Spain.

short: Possibly Saint Einhildis of Niedermünster.
note: Possibly Saint Einhildis, also called Einhild, an eighth-century religious woman associated with Niedermünster in Alsace.

sources.label: Catholic Church in Norway · Gundelinda of Niedermünster

short: Possibly Saint Petronax, restorer of Monte Cassino.
note: Possibly Saint Petronax, an eighth-century Benedictine abbot who restored Monte Cassino after its destruction and became known as its second founder.

short: Possibly Saint Guibert, founder of Gembloux Abbey.
note: Possibly Saint Guibert, a tenth-century founder of the Benedictine abbey at Gembloux, in present-day Belgium. He later lived as a monk at Gorze.

sources.label: French Bishops’ Conference · Guibert of Gembloux

short: Possibly Eigil, abbot of Fulda and biographer of Saint Sturm.
note: Possibly Eigil of Fulda, a ninth-century Benedictine abbot and author of a life of Saint Sturm, Fulda’s founder.

short: Possibly Saint Grimkeld, one of the Crowland martyrs.
note: Possibly Saint Grimkeld, one of the monks remembered among the martyrs of Crowland Abbey, traditionally killed during a ninth-century Viking raid.

sources.label: Catholic Church in Norway · Theodore and the Crowland martyrs

short: Possibly Saint Gracia, one of the martyrs of Alzira.
note: Possibly Saint Gracia, one of three sibling martyrs honored at Alzira in Spain, alongside Bernard and Maria.

sources.label: City of Alzira · Cultural heritage inventory

short: Possibly Saint Lybe, a martyr of Palmyra.
note: Possibly Saint Lybe, a Christian martyr traditionally commemorated at Palmyra with Eutropia and Leonis during the Roman persecutions.

short: Possibly Saint Lollian, one of the Seven Martyrs of Samosata.
note: Possibly Saint Lollian, one of the Seven Martyrs of Samosata commemorated in Syriac Christian tradition. Their collective life survives in Syriac manuscripts.

short: Possibly Saint Anian, the saint commemorated at Saint-Chinian.
note: Possibly Saint Anian, the saint to whom the medieval abbey at Saint-Chinian in southern France was dedicated.

short: Possibly Saint Branwalader, also called Brélade.
note: Possibly Saint Branwalader, also called Branwallader or Brélade, an early Celtic saint associated with Cornwall and the Channel Islands. St Brélade on Jersey preserves his name.

sources.label: Catholic Church in Norway · Saint Branwalader

short: Possibly Egino of Chur, a twelfth-century bishop.
note: Possibly Egino of Chur, a twelfth-century bishop in what is now Switzerland, associated with Emperor Frederick Barbarossa.

short: Possibly Saint Ia, a martyr of Persia.
note: Possibly Saint Ia, a Christian woman venerated as a martyr of the Persian persecutions under Shapur II in the fourth century.

sources.label: Orthodox Church in America · Saint Ia

short: Possibly Saint Tanco, traditionally a bishop of Verden.
note: Possibly Saint Tanco, also called Tancho, an early saint traditionally counted among the bishops of Verden in Germany. His surviving life is largely legendary.

sources.label: Catholic Church in Norway · Saint Tanco

short: Possibly Saint Alchmund, a Northumbrian prince and martyr.
note: Possibly Saint Alchmund, also spelled Alcmund, a Northumbrian prince venerated as a martyr after his death around 800. His shrine became an important religious site at Derby.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Saint Gaudentius, bishop of Brescia.
note: Possibly Saint Gaudentius of Brescia, an early Christian bishop and preacher ordained by Ambrose of Milan. A collection of his sermons survives.

sources.label: French Bishops’ Conference · Gaudentius of Brescia

short: Possibly Pinianus, a late Roman Christian ascetic.
note: Possibly Pinianus, a late Roman Christian ascetic and husband of Melania the Younger, known for renouncing his fortune. Augustine’s letters describe attempts to persuade him to become a priest at Hippo.

short: Possibly Askr, the first man in Norse mythology.
note: Possibly Askr, whose name means ash tree, the first man in Norse mythology. In the Prose Edda, the gods shape him and the first woman, Embla, from trees found beside the sea.

short: Possibly the phoenix, the bird of renewal.
note: Possibly the phoenix, a fabulous bird in Greek and Roman accounts whose death produces a new phoenix. Its long life and association with the sun made it an enduring emblem of renewal.

sources.label: Classical accounts of the phoenix · Theoi

short: Possibly Hesperos, the evening star personified.
note: Possibly Hesperos, the Greek personification of the evening star: the planet Venus seen after sunset. Eosphoros or Phosphoros names its morning appearance.

sources.label: Classical sources on Hesperos and Eosphoros · Theoi

short: Possibly Gaia, the Greek personification of Earth.
note: Possibly Gaia, also spelled Gaea or Gea, the Greek personification of Earth. In Hesiod’s Theogony she is a primordial deity and the mother of Ouranos and the Titans.

sources.label: Hesiod and other classical sources on Gaia · Theoi

short: Possibly an Erinys, one of the Greek Furies.
note: Possibly an Erinys, singular of Erinyes: the Greek avenging goddesses often called Furies in English. They punish grave offenses, especially bloodshed within a family and violations of sworn obligations.

sources.label: Classical sources on the Erinyes · Theoi

short: Possibly Greek moira, an allotted share or fate.
note: Possibly Greek moira, an allotted share and, by extension, a person’s fate. The Moirai personify destiny, usually as three goddesses who spin, measure, and cut the thread of life.

sources.label: Classical sources on the Moirai · Theoi

short: Possibly Paeon, the physician of the Greek gods.
note: Possibly Paeon, the physician of the gods in Greek epic. Related forms of the name also serve as titles of Apollo in his role as healer.

short: Possibly Phlegethon, a fiery river of the Greek underworld.
note: Possibly Phlegethon, also called Pyriphlegethon, a river of fire in Greek accounts of the underworld. Its name is connected with burning.

short: Possibly the fifty daughters of Danaus.
note: Possibly the Danaides, the fifty daughters of Danaus in Greek mythology. All but Hypermnestra killed their husbands on their wedding night; she spared Lynceus.

short: Possibly Abraxas, a mystical name linked with Gnosticism.
note: Possibly Abraxas, also written Abrasax, a mystical name associated with Basilidian Gnosticism. Its Greek letter values total 365, the number of heavens in an ancient account of that teaching.

short: Possibly Adonai, a Hebrew divine title meaning “my Lord.”
note: Possibly Adonai, a Hebrew title of God conventionally translated “my Lord” or “Lord.” It names God as lord of the world.

short: Possibly the apeiron, Anaximander’s boundless first principle.
note: Possibly the apeiron, the boundless or indefinite source of things in the philosophy of Anaximander. It is an inexhaustible origin from which the world’s contrasting elements emerge.

sources.label: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy · Presocratic Philosophy

short: Possibly Arioch, a royal officer in the Book of Daniel.
note: Possibly Arioch, the chief of Nebuchadnezzar’s guard in Daniel 2. Charged with killing Babylon’s wise men, he instead brings Daniel before the king to interpret the royal dream.

short: Possibly the land of Nod, Cain’s place of exile.
note: Possibly the land of Nod in Genesis 4:16, where Cain settles east of Eden after his exile. The name echoes a Hebrew word for wandering.

short: Possibly the Paraclete, the advocate or helper.
note: Possibly the Paraclete, from Greek paraklētos, an advocate or someone called to another’s aid. In the Gospel of John the title is applied to the Holy Spirit.

sources.label: John Paul II · The Holy Spirit as Paraclete

short: Possibly Camena, a Roman name for a Muse.
note: Possibly Camena, also written Camoena, a Roman name for a Muse. The Camenae were associated with song and with a sacred grove outside Rome.

short: Possibly Yuruparí, an ancestral being in Amazonian traditions.
note: Possibly Yuruparí, also written Jurupari, an ancestral being in traditions of the northwest Amazon. Among communities of Colombia’s Pirá Paraná River, he is described as an anaconda who lived as a person and is represented by sacred trumpets.

sources.label: UNESCO · Traditional knowledge of the jaguar shamans of Yuruparí

short: Possibly gandharvas, celestial musicians of Indian tradition.
note: Possibly gandharvas, celestial musicians in Indian religious traditions. They are often represented in sculpture and painting as heavenly attendants making music.

sources.label: Metropolitan Museum of Art · Celestial Musician (Gandharva)

short: Possibly the sefirot, ten divine attributes in Kabbalah.
note: Possibly the sefirot, ten attributes or emanations through which the divine is expressed in Kabbalah. They include wisdom, understanding, loving-kindness, strength, and beauty.

short: Possibly Savitar, a solar deity of the Rigveda.
note: Possibly Savitar, a Vedic deity associated with the sun’s animating power. Rigvedic hymns describe him traveling in a golden chariot, bringing light and setting living beings to rest.

short: Possibly Surya, the Hindu sun god.
note: Possibly Surya, the Hindu sun god, praised in the Rigveda and represented in religious art as a source of light. Lotus flowers are among his characteristic attributes.

short: Possibly Sanskrit caitanya, consciousness or spirit.
note: Possibly Sanskrit caitanya, meaning consciousness, intelligence, or spirit. In philosophical usage it can denote the universal consciousness or soul.

short: Possibly Fauna, the Roman goddess associated with Bona Dea.
note: Possibly Fauna, an ancient Roman goddess identified with Bona Dea, the “Good Goddess.” Her worship included rites reserved for women.

sources.label: Platner and Ashby · Bona Dea Subsaxana

short: Possibly Venant, a traditional name associated with Regulus.
note: Possibly Venant, a star-name associated with Regulus in Leo in historical accounts of Persian astronomy. Regulus is one of the stars grouped as the four royal stars or guardians of the sky.

sources.label: Royal Astronomical Society of Canada · World Asterisms Project

short: Possibly Saint Barbara, the patron saint of artillery.
note: Possibly Saint Barbara, a Christian martyr traditionally invoked by artillerymen and workers in other dangerous occupations. Reliable details of her life are scarce.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Blessed Oringa, a medieval Tuscan religious woman.
note: Possibly Blessed Oringa, a medieval Tuscan woman venerated for a life of religious devotion and humble domestic service.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Maxentius, the Roman emperor in Catherine’s legend.
note: Possibly the Roman emperor Maxentius, who appears in the medieval legend of Saint Catherine of Alexandria as the ruler who orders her imprisonment and execution.

sources.label: Metropolitan Museum of Art · Saint Catherine of Alexandria

short: Possibly Saint Macarius the Great, an Egyptian monastic founder.
note: Possibly Saint Macarius the Great, also called Abu Makar, an Egyptian desert ascetic associated with early monastic life. His relics are venerated at the monastery bearing his name in Wadi El-Natrun.

sources.label: ICCROM · Wadi El-Natrun and the monastery of Saint Macarius
Monastery of Saint Macarius · Church and relics

short: Possibly Helios, the Greek sun god.
note: Possibly Helios, the Greek personification of the sun, traditionally pictured driving a radiant chariot across the sky.

sources.label: Homeric and other classical sources on Helios · Theoi

short: Possibly Hyperion, the Titan associated with heavenly light.
note: Possibly Hyperion, a Greek Titan and, in Hesiod, the father of Helios the sun, Selene the moon, and Eos the dawn. Ancient poets also use Hyperion as a name for the sun itself.

sources.label: Classical sources on Helios and Hyperion · Theoi

short: The Dog Star, the brightest star in Earth’s night sky.
note: Sirius, the Dog Star in Canis Major, is the brightest star in Earth’s night sky. It is a binary system: the brilliant Sirius A has a faint white-dwarf companion, Sirius B.

sources.label: NASA · Sirius, the brightest star in the night

short: Possibly Saint Goscelinus, abbot of San Solutore.
note: Possibly Saint Goscelinus, also called Goslin or Gozzelinus, a Benedictine abbot of San Solutore near Turin in northern Italy.

sources.label: Catholic Church in Norway · Goscelinus of Turin

short: Of the open ocean.
note: Relating to the open ocean, especially waters away from the shore.

short: Foul-smelling or blackened by smoke.
note: An archaic adjective meaning foul-smelling, rancid, or blackened by smoke. It belongs to the same word family as reek.

short: Of the sea, especially an inland sea.
note: Relating to the sea, particularly an inland sea and the lands around it; from Greek thalassa, sea.

short: The rail around a ship’s stern.
note: A rail around the stern of a ship; also the upper part of a wooden ship’s stern.

short: A small container for consecrated bread.
note: A vessel for keeping the consecrated bread of the Eucharist. The word also names a box holding sample coins for tests of their metal and weight.

short: A clock designed for precise timekeeping.
note: An older term for a clock designed to maintain exceptionally accurate time.

short: A barracks or soldiers’ lodging.
note: A barracks or building that lodges soldiers in a garrison; from French caserne.

short: A light carriage.
note: A small, light carriage, commonly drawn by one horse; the term has also been used for a covered cart.

short: A ruler’s private circle of advisers.
note: A small, private group of advisers influencing a ruler; by extension, a secretive political clique. The Spanish word originally means a small room.

short: Tinder prepared from tree-growing fungi.
note: A soft, spongy material prepared from certain fungi growing on trees and used as tinder.

short: Kinship or relationship; legally, descent through the male line.
note: Kinship or relationship, including a relationship of common origin; in legal usage, descent reckoned through the male line.

short: A wish too weak to become action.
note: A faint wish or inclination that does not develop into a decision or an effort to act. From Latin velle, to wish or will.

short: Fever.
note: A medical term for fever, an abnormally elevated body temperature.

short: An underlying reality or distinct divine person.
note: The underlying substance or reality of something. In Christian theology, a distinct person of the Trinity; the plural is hypostases.

short: A long cloak, often hooded.
note: A long cloak or overcoat, especially one fitted with a hood.

short: A roofed gallery open on one or more sides.
note: A covered gallery forming part of a building, open to the air along one or more sides.

short: A cavalry standard-bearer; also a brass instrument.
note: Historically, a junior cavalry officer who carried the troop’s standard, or the standard itself. Cornet also names a trumpet-like musical instrument.

short: A fragrant flower; also a purple color or bloodstone.
note: A plant of the genus Heliotropium, especially a cultivated kind with fragrant flowers. The word also names a grayish-purple color and the gemstone bloodstone.

short: A vivid cherry-red color.
note: A bright red resembling ripe cherries; from the French word for cherry.

short: A swift falcon; also wandering or foreign.
